facts.claim: Motel Mayday was released on April 2, 2021 on Yucatan Records and has 11 tracks.
The title track 'Motel Mayday' is credited to Josiah Leming as writer and composer and runs about 3:58.
The title track started the journey that led to the album. It was first recorded as demos in the mountains north of Los Angeles.
The album was then recorded in London with producer Duncan Mills, whose credits include Jake Bugg, The Hunna and The Vaccines.
Motel Mayday is the second album by Josiah and the Bonnevilles and the sixth by the singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist behind the band.
The band's debut, On Trial, came out in 2018, but Motel Mayday was already well underway by then.
Josiah signed with the British indie label Yucatan and came to London to complete the album.
The label describes the album's themes as girls, cars, bars and bad decisions, written about in retrospect with humour rather than remorse.
Josiah grew up in Morristown, Tennessee, and moved to Atlanta at 16 after leaving school. He auditioned for American Idol and was offered a Warner Brothers deal without reaching the final 24.
Josiah and the Bonnevilles is the project of American musician Josiah Leming, born March 26, 1989. He gained a backing band during a residency in L.A.

research.lineage: The band sits in an American alt-country, folk and Americana singer-songwriter tradition, and its Motel Mayday album was made with a British indie label and a London producer.

draft:
The chorus of **Motel Mayday** never changes its mind, but who it's aimed at does. "I should have known better, I should have stayed away," the narrator sings, and he means it. Then in the second verse the line comes back with one word swapped. Now it's "you should have known better," and it belongs to the Lord, answering a man who has just picked a fight with heaven over how much he hates the road. That small change of pronoun is the whole song in miniature: a man trying to file his own bad decisions as somebody else's fault, and being handed them right back.

What pulls him under each time isn't glamour. "She bought me beer and she knew my name," he sings, and the second half of that line does the damage. After the hangover, the fight with his baby and a night slept off by the side of the road, being recognized is the drug. She sings along to every song. For someone who feels this alone, that's enough to follow her anywhere.

Josiah Leming wrote it, and the record's label describes the album's girls, cars, bars and bad decisions as looked back on with humour rather than remorse. There's humour here, sure ("Jim Beam is a friend of mine"), but the last verse lets the guard down. A girl in Tennessee has a baby that looks like him, so he's headed back up the mountain to send money home. Then comes the swing he can't steady: "Some days I drink til I'm barely alive." Shame and duty sit next to each other and neither one wins. The motel is still waiting when the chorus comes around again.

The band plays it straight, which suits the confession. Strummed acoustic guitar and a clean, arpeggiated electric line ride over a walking bass and a steady kick-snare-hi-hat beat, all at an easy, moderate pace. The vocal is clear and conversational, a little melancholic, with no harmonies to soften it. The room sounds open, and the production is polished without hiding anything.

That polish has a story. The song began as demos in the mountains north of Los Angeles and started the journey toward the album, which Leming finished in London for the British indie Yucatan with producer Duncan Mills, whose credits include Jake Bugg and The Vaccines. So it's an American alt-country road song, with Americana's barroom confessions, cut clean on the other side of the Atlantic.

You keep singing along because the chorus lets you feel exactly what he feels: knowing better, and going anyway.
